question: An 80-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of a decreasing level of consciousness. He had blurred vision for several days. Two weeks ago, he had transient numbness in the right arm for 3 days. He was diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance 2 years ago. He is not fully alert. His temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 75/min, respiratory rate is 13/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. He has gingival bleeding. Cervical lymphadenopathy is noted on palpation. Both the liver and spleen are palpated 6 cm below the costal margins. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is shown. Urine electrophoresis shows no abnormalities. A skeletal survey shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance" -> "increased risk of multiple myeloma" -> "possible hyperviscosity syndrome" -> 70% CHAIN: "Hyperviscosity syndrome" -> "neurological symptoms like altered mental status and blurred vision" -> "possible cause of decreasing level of consciousness" -> 80% CHAIN: "Gingival bleeding" -> "suggestive of coagulopathy" -> "possible hyperviscosity syndrome-related coagulopathy" -> 70% CHAIN: "Liver and spleen palpable below costal margins" -> "suggestive of organomegaly" -> "possible infiltration by abnormal plasma cells" -> 60% CHAIN: "Cervical lymphadenopathy" -> "suggestive of lymphoproliferative disorder" -> "consistent with monoclonal gammopathy" -> 80% CHAIN: "Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation" -> "confirmatory test for monoclonal gammopathy" -> "helps in diagnosis and management decision" -> 90% CHAIN: "Urine electrophoresis normal" -> "rules out light chain deposition disease" -> "less likely cause of symptoms" -> 80% CHAIN: "Skeletal survey normal" -> "rules out lytic bone lesions" -> "less likely multiple myeloma" -> 70%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation with neurological symptoms, gingival bleeding, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy is concerning for hyperviscosity syndrome related to monoclonal gammopathy. Given the risk of hyperviscosity-related complications, the most appropriate next step in management would be plasmapheresis to rapidly reduce the circulating abnormal proteins and improve symptoms.
